utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-98-33-A, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Norman Farrell for the Prosecution, and with me is Mr. Wolfgang Sakulin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For the appellant?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, my learned friend. I'm Nenad Petrusic, from the Defence of General Krstic, and during the appeal proceeding I will have Mr. Visnjic appearing with me and Mr. Norman Sepenuk, who has joined us in the appeal proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. General Krstic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? You have to turn your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we cannot hear the translation into B/C/S. We cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Number 6, channel number 6. Are you getting a translation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand, General? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is the first Status Conference in the appeal, being held pursuant to Rule 65 bis. If I may turn immediately to the issue of the condition of the appellant. Is there anything which counsel on his behalf wish to raise about the conditions of his detention or any other matter relating to his mental or physical condition? Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the state of Mr. Krstic and his treatment at the Detention Unit, nothing has changed substantially. Problems are evident. They are there all the time. A few days ago an orthopaedic specialist examined Mr. Krstic, his leg, and he came to the conclusion that in detention conditions there are no technical possibilities for carrying out so-called hydrotherapy, which is indispensable. There is a certain process in the leg that creates problems and is painful to Mr. Krstic. Now, how will this problem be resolved? The Defence will try to look into this matter through the appropriate medical services of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand, though, don't you, that this is a matter which you have to raise first with the commanding officer of the Detention Unit. Then, if you don't receive satisfaction from him, you have an avenue of appeal to the President of the Tribunal. It's not something within the powers of the Appeals Chamber to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. I fully concur. But I have just answered your question related to the current condition of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. That's what the Rule provides for us to ask. But then having asked it, usually there's very little that we are able to do in relation to any complaints except to draw your attention to the fact that it's a matter for the commanding officer initially, and then after that, the President. Right. Now, in relation to the preparation for the appeal, the first thing to be dealt with is your motion for an extension of time. Have you read the decision on that point in Kordic and Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, as for this question and these submissions that are before you, Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Sepenuk have been dealing with these matters to a greater extent. I have been dealing with other matters related to the appeal. So by your leave, I would like to give the floor to Mr. Visnjic in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we have looked at most of the decisions passed by the Appeals Chamber, and I don't know which decision you specifically have in mind as related to Kordic Cerkez, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is one called "Decision on Second Motions to Extend Time for Filing Appellants' Briefs." It's dated the 2nd of July, 2001, in which it makes it clear that new evidence matters will not be sufficient basis for delaying an appellant's brief. And there's been a subsequent decision, I think only a day or so ago, in Blaskic, whereas Mr. Blaskic was entitled, was permitted to delay matters rather an extraordinarily long time. He's now being required to get on with it. You see, I think that as a previous advocate, I understand the desire of anybody to have the perfect appellant's brief, but we don't live under perfect conditions here. And the stand has been taken that you are required to file your appellant's brief so that we know what he's all about, and then you will be permitted to add to it when the matters about new evidence have crystallised. The only other matter is the addition to your team. Actually, I had not realised that your American colleague was going to appear as counsel in the matter. He's regarded by the Registrar, I understand, as a consultant, but I'm not sure how you can use that to your advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. The Registry has registered him as a consultant. Perhaps we have not defined this precisely enough at the outset, but our colleague is a consultant, and we availed ourselves of this opportunity since we had a meeting here, all of us together. We wanted to appear in court, all of us, so that the Court would be in a position to get all necessary information or all required information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I don't think you've answered my question. You see, you rely upon the new evidence and the addition to your team of a consultant to extend the time for filing your appellant's brief. Now, in both Kordic and Blaskic, that approach has failed in relation to new evidence, and I am not sure why there should be any difference because you now have a new member of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one of the reasons or, rather, one of the factors that we have relied upon is the fact that the case is so voluminous and there is such a great amount of material to be dealt with in the appeal. So this just supports our case. Rather, the two reasons you refer to are two additional reasons that we have been referring to, namely, that our new consultant has to look into all of this, and we wanted to link all of this up with the new evidence as well. However, at any rate, I believe that the abundance of material in this case -- and also the Registry can provide information as to when the Defence really started working on the appeal, bearing in mind when we actually got the decision. So bearing in mind this entire framework, we have put all of this into a single motion for extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand, don't you, you've already received one extension in which the voluminous nature of the material you're dealing with was taken into account. So what you're asking us is to reconsider the decision that was made before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to indicate certain circumstances that had not been looked into until now. For example, the circumstance that the Defence -- actually, I can say this now within this request, that Mr. Petrusic and I have been working on this case incessantly since December 1999, that is to say, when the trial was announced. So it was two years altogether, really, until July 2001. Then we got the decision very quickly after that. That was the 2nd of August. And we simply were not in a position, we were not physically capable and professionally capable of starting to work on the case immediately. We started working sometime in September, and that can be checked with the Registry because we have been making submissions to them related to this. Another thing that I wish to draw your attention to is that with regard to certain elements related to the appeal, we noted them only subsequently, after consulting General Krstic, and this was upon receipt of the decision, the decision in the Serbo-Croat language, that is. Bearing in mind the contribution of Mr. Sepenuk as his view in terms of the additional time needed for the appeal, we have brought all of this together into this one motion. It does require perhaps a few months, but basically I'm talking about the beginning of September until the present day. Of course, all of this includes the appeal filed by the Prosecutor or, rather, the time that is needed for his response or, rather, responding to him, and of course due to that, we face additional difficulties and we can observe that now. For example, some texts in the Swedish language, et cetera. However, I think this is of secondary importance with regard to our motion. The core of the matter is insufficient time. This is the first ever judgement that relates to genocide, and the literature that we have available is primarily in the English language, and actually, within all the circumstances that Mr. Petrusic and I have been working, we really felt it was necessary to seek the assistance of Mr. Sepenuk as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you see, the Registrar has given permission for him to join the team in order to assist you on this issue of genocide, not generally in relation to the appeal. That's why I expressed some surprise to see him now here as a member of the team in court. And it was very limited on that basis. I don't understand why his addition to the team should give you further time to enable him to do work for which he's not been retained. And as for your suggestion this is the first decision on genocide, it's clearly not the first decision on genocide. The Rwanda Tribunal has brought in several decision on genocide. It is the first one for this Tribunal, certainly, but there are other decisions of a recent nature dealing with genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I was not precise enough. I meant the first decision on genocide in this Tribunal and the first judgement on genocide in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand all that. Is there anything you want to add to this issue about extensions of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly like to ask you to hear the reasons that would be put forth by Mr. Sepenuk, and this has to deal with the part of the proceedings that he would be involved in. I think it will be very brief, and we won't take up too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if I do so, I want to make it very clear I am prepared to listen to him speak to us, to the Tribunal, as a consultant. That's the basis upon which he's here. I'm happy to hear him on that basis. But I don't want there to be some reliance placed subsequently upon my having done so in order to change his status.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think this is quite clear to us, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Sepenuk, what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My understanding, Your Honour, of my consultant's role in the case I think is a little bit broader than what Your Honour has stated. I've been retained to analyse the entire record in the case to identify any issue that could be raised on appeal. We know that the genocide issue is going to be raised, so that's been focused on, and that no doubt will be a very main issue on this appeal. But before I can identify any other issues on the appeal, and before we can intelligently focus in on genocide, it's absolutely basic, as I'm sure Your Honour well appreciates, that I read the over 10.000 pages of the trial record. There's also literally thousands of pages contained in the various exhibits in the case. May I offer just one other issue, Your Honour, that I think will be raised on the appeal. That's the very difficult issue that Your Honour has already dealt with in the Talic case, interpreting the Tadic decision on joint criminal enterprise, and that is to say where an alleged crime is committed outside the scope of the alleged criminal enterprise. For example, if there is a forcible deportation, as the government has proved in this case - at least, General Krstic is now convicted of that - followed by so-called opportunistic killings, the Trial Chamber in this case found General Krstic liable for those killings on the basis that under the Talic and Tadic rationales, the General should have foreseen that that was a consequence of the forced bussing. We respectfully submit, Your Honour - at least, we're going to submit, I'm sure - that that's too broad a concept, that it's too much of a jump from one to the other. It's a very, very difficult issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you mean as a matter of law or factually in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Certainly factually, Your Honour, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because we are bound by the decision in Tadic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- Tadic, and in Talic all we sought to do was to explain it. So in Tadic, that's what they use as the test. The common law test, as I understand it, is whether the crime, which is outside the object of the joint criminal enterprise, was one which was reasonably contemplated by the parties. Now, I'm not sure that I see any difference between that and the one which the Appeals Chamber accepted in Tadic, but whatever it is, we're bound by that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, so I say, first, factually there's no doubt we're going to try to distinguish it, but I also say that at the very least, we may suggest to the Appeals Chamber in this case that perhaps this is too broad a concept and perhaps the Appeals Chamber might want to take another look at it, based on authorities that we would present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But then, you see, you run into a problem that the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski and in Celebici confirmed that the Appeals Chamber is bound by its previous decisions, except in very limited circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So I suggest to you, you should not spend a lot of your time at this stage arguing or seeking to put an argument that Tadic was wrong, because the Appeals Chamber has said it will be bound by its previous decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I do appreciate that. But as I say, at the very least, we'll be making certain factual arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But to make the factual arguments I have to read, as I say, this 10.000-page record, literally thousands of pages of exhibits, and Your Honour, this is a very formidable opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is not something which is new. This has always been the issue in the appeal, whether the factual findings are correct, so that your two colleagues have had plenty of opportunity of considering that. And having three counsel, it is not generally regarded as being efficient for each of them to read the whole of the record. You divide the work up between you. So you have a problem in trying to persuade the Appeals Chamber here that you should get extra time because you have come into it late. You're here as the consultant. I accept that there may be some imprecision in the use of the word "consultant," but it is to advise on genocide, from the common law point of view, and certainly perhaps other matters from a common law point of view. But the slogging hard work of reading through the whole record has been done by your two colleagues. They were in the trial, and they should be able to direct you, or you can ask them to direct you to particular parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I certainly have been directed to particular parts, Your Honour, but I did think it essential, and I do think it essential, very respectfully to Your Honour, to get my own assessment of what the case is all about, even on the genocide issue, where the question of intent is going to be paramount. And as we pointed out in our memorandum, the literature on the subject is absolutely vast, and the issue, I think, is a paramount one. I do think -- I hope this is not -- I don't mean it as hyperbole, but I do think that this will be perhaps as significant a decision on genocide as there ever has been. And I take it very seriously. I find it a very awesome task. And we'd like to submit a work product that's equal to the dignity of the work product produced by the Trial Chamber, and unless we have time to do that, Your Honour, we're not going to be able to produce that kind of a work product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was a phrase that I used in the Kordic case, that everybody likes to have the absolutely perfect appellant's brief, but we cannot afford this sort of thing. Your client is sitting in detention, in conditions of difficulty because of the state of his leg, and you are asking him, in effect, to sit there for longer to enable you to polish something which perhaps could have been expressed in a more fluent way. I don't really think that that's the way we can operate. We operate on the basis we get proper assistance from counsel, and they have the opportunity of addressing us orally at the hearing, they have the opportunity of adding to their written briefs, especially after new evidence points have been involved, and we just have to get on. At the moment, neither the Prosecution nor the Appeals Chamber has any idea of the matters that are going to be litigated. And this has been demonstrated to be a wholly improper approach in Blaskic, where the matter has just languished for years because the appellant was never forced to put on his appellant's brief. Now, that's where we stand at the moment. We are absolutely ignorant of what's going to happen, and we've got to know. But anyway, I understand what you put, and it will be, as you say, a very interesting and perhaps a very important judgement, and we want all the assistance we can get, but we really must insist on having it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The other matter from the point of view of the appellant: You want to delay your response to the Prosecution's appeal, your respondent's brief to the Prosecution's appeal, because you say it will raise the same issues as you are going to raise in your appeal. I'm not sure that I understand that. The Prosecution, in its appeal, has raised a number of issues, saying that the Trial Chamber proceeded upon the impermissible basis that there should be some sort of a categorisation of sentences starting with certain particular people at the very top and everybody else has to be lower, rather than just looking at the worst category of case, which is what, I must confess, I've always understood to be the law, but we have yet to work that one out, and they have stressed all the matters of aggravation that the Trial Chamber is asserted not to have given proper consideration to. Now, your response to that brief will be to point out that there are also a great deal of matters of mitigation which you also are going to say in your appeal were not properly taken into account. I do not understand why you can't do it now. It doesn't depend in any way upon new evidence. It's just a matter you have to put on a response to the Prosecution's appeal, and when you come on to your own appeal, you can refer back to your submissions there and include them by reference in your own appellant's brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do appreciate the force of your comments. It was suggested merely as a way of streamlining the case: instead of two briefs, one brief. We are going to argue -- I know enough about the case at this point, Your Honour, to know that we're going to ask the Court to reverse, the Tribunal to reverse the genocide judgement. If the Court -- if the Tribunal does not do that, we're then going to ask for a reduction of the 46-year sentence largely on the basis of our analysis of the genocide case, and other factors in the case, and in doing that, we'll necessarily deal with the Prosecutor's arguments on genocidal factors that go into a sentence. We just thought it would be a cleaner, more streamlined way of doing it. It's not the end of the world, Your Honour if you ask us to submit a brief now. We would prefer to do it at a later time. Hopefully, Your Honour, at a much later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a very appealing way of putting it, Mr. Sepenuk, but I'd glad to say that you realise the inevitability of having to put on a respondent's brief, because I'm afraid that's what you'll be ordered to do. As to the period, we have yet to deal with that. Is there anything else that you want to add on that particular matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Farrell, do you want to respond to any of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. Most of the issues you've addressed, and our response has been filed yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, now, the other matter was this application for access. You have asked for a hearing, an oral hearing, before me. I should emphasise, this is not a decision which I will be making as the Pre-Appeal Judge. It's a matter for the whole Appeals Chamber, access to documents. If you are in some way of the opinion that it's going to assist you, I would like to have something in writing to demonstrate why the arguments can't be put in writing. They are usually put in writing with no oral argument. And it's an issue where you've now got an enormously detailed response from the Prosecution, which I received this morning and which I haven't finished reading, and I see that as I walked into court I was handed a document which apparently is your reply to it. I'm not sure that it was wise of you to have rushed into a reply so brief to such a detailed response. But my point is, I can't hear the argument. It would have to be by the whole Appeals Chamber. And in order for you to get an order for oral hearing, you've got to demonstrate why it is a matter that can't be dealt with in writing, for example, by a more detailed reply. I have to say I haven't read this reply because I haven't read the response, but I've just noticed it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we gave this reply as our contribution to shortening the Status Conference today. Taking into account that we received a fairly comprehensive submission from the Prosecution, we thought that we would provide this in response to their long list of issues in light of the newly discovered evidence pursuant to Rule 68. And we were contemplating another submission, and listening to your comments now, that is very much in tune with what we had in mind. And as I said, we have provided this to you and to the Prosecution, expecting that perhaps there will be a decision or ruling made today. If not, if this is not the case, we are prepared to submit a longer, more comprehensive motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There can't be a decision today because I have no power to determine, but there is one thing that you say there which I think I should draw your attention to now. You have, in effect, invited me as the Pre-Appeal Judge to sit down and read through all of the material which you want from the Prosecution to determine, in effect as your agent, that you have a legitimate forensic purpose to inspect it. You're not going to get an order along those lines. It has never been the task of a judge to determine those matters. The only task the judge has to perform is whether there's some balancing problem with public interest immunity or some state privilege, and even then the judge does not do it until after the legitimate forensic purpose has been demonstrated, and the legitimate forensic purpose is the one that has been discussed already in a number of these cases. It is for you to demonstrate that there is, to use a fairly general phrase, a likelihood that you will be assisted in the Prosecution of your appeal by having access to the documents. It's not for the judges to look at the documents themselves to work that out for you. So when you do your written submissions, your further submissions, may I suggest that you concentrate on what I think is now the generally accepted test that it is likely that you will be assisted in the Prosecution of your appeal if you have access to the material which you seek. Now, the response by the Prosecution, as I say, I haven't read it very carefully, but there is a very detailed response there which I think you may have to take paragraph by paragraph to point out to us what you say will be some error in relation to what they have said. Your argument about equality of arms has been left to one side in most of the decisions. If it has to be determined in this case, it will be an interesting point because it will run counter to everything that has been said so far. I think I warned you about that. How long would you like in order to put your more detailed reply onto the Prosecution's response?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same amount of time that was given to the Prosecution to respond to our submission, which means ten days, if that was the deadline given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that will be just before the non-Orthodox Christmas. So I suppose seeing that as we have plenty of applications for the delay of trials at the beginning of the year in order to enable the Orthodox members of the bar to celebrate Christmas with their families, you should at least have the disadvantage of having to work right up to the non-Orthodox Christmas. That will make it the 21st. The 21st is a Friday, from memory. Perhaps we'll give you until the 24th. Well, I'll make an order then that I extend it until the 24th of December for a more detailed reply to the Prosecution's response in relation of a motion for access to the documents. The decision on the application for extension of time may be given to you by that time. I'm not quite sure whether I can get all the judges together to discuss it, but I shall certainly attempt to do so. Is there anything else you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like one thing, if you would take -- if you would want to take into account just one other aspect. During the -- the regular procedure would be the Prosecution's briefs and then our response. Now, what is happening in the appeal of the Prosecution happens to coincide with our own appellant's brief, which is 30 days, and dealing with that now takes away some time from our own brief. So I would like the Trial Chamber to perhaps take into account that particular circumstance when reaching a decision. It's a matter of simple mathematics, really, but I just wanted to point it out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, if I may say so, this issue has been available for you to consider ever since the judgement was given. The Prosecution made it very clear that they were going to appeal. You could have gotten well under way with any response to that brief already instead of attempting to get it all delayed. I'm not sure that you'll get a very sympathetic hearing, having put it to one side, as it were, you should now be given extra time. Are you able to tell me when the 30 days expires? That's the response to the Prosecution appellant's brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14th of December, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's in three days' time. Well, Mr. Farrell, have you got any suggestion in relation to that? I don't feel like giving in to, in effect, fait accompli, but I'm not sure we'll get very much assistance from something which is produced in three days' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand what you said, and the Prosecution's position was somewhat more eloquently articulated by you in your questioning in light of the three-day time limit which we're going to bring to your attention. Obviously, there's not much we can do in the circumstances. The only thing that I'd ask that you consider is that the scheduling of the members of my section, in light of the coming holidays, was that if the brief was to be coming in on the 14th of December, we had scheduled the time frame of the period we have to file our reply. If, for example, it's postponed for a week or two, then we will be in a difficult position in terms of trying to schedule the time we require to file our reply. That's all I wanted to bring to your attention on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was thinking of making it the end of next week, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's what I was afraid of, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That will cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, we can certainly try and comply, and if not, we'll file an extension of time. I'm sorry, a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps I should reveal that I will be the vacation Judge for the second and third weeks of vacation, seeing as I'm one of the few Judges who lives here -- well, at least on the basis of the distance to travel is too far, so I have to live here. So that you'll get a sympathetic hearing from the vacation Judge if you want an extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll inform the vacation Judge as soon as we receive it if we need it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think what I shall do then, I will extend the time for the response to the Prosecution's appellant's brief to the 21st of December, and I'll -- I'll make that order now. The other decision will have to be given as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I say this, needless to say, with the greatest of respect for the Court, and I'd like to find out if there's any chance at all that Your Honour might be persuaded to grant a bit more time. I expect to be taking a prominent part in that preparation. I have commitments for the next several days in the United States. And I appreciate your comments -- Your Honour's comments about a perfect brief. That certainly resonates with me. And much as I'd love to present a perfect brief - we all would - we know that's not going to happen. But we at least want to present an adequate and competent brief, Your Honour, and we're wondering if you could at least give us until January 10th, which is the date when our initial brief is due. If you could give us until January 10th to file an answering brief, I think we could at least get a competent brief by then, Your Honour, and then as much time thereafter as Your Honour sees fit on the filing of our initial brief. And again, this is a Herculean task, Your Honour, it truly is, to do a real job in this case. We want to present at the very least a competent and adequate brief to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Sepenuk, may I just emphasise this is response to the Prosecution's appeal in relation to sentencing. This is not anything that needs anything more than an answer to their complaints that the Trial Chamber, having made the findings that it did, has not made -- given a high enough sentence. Now, that doesn't require an attack upon the findings by you. You'll do that in your appellant's brief. And if I -- if I give you the relief you are now seeking, what I'm doing is granting the application that you have made to have the two of them filed together. I don't know whether you realise that, but what you're doing is, in effect, getting the relief to which I've already indicated I don't think you're entitled to delay it until your own brief is due.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As I understand it, Your Honour, you've taken under submission the question of when our brief is due. You intend to rule on that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that your brief at the present --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Our opening brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your own appellant's brief, in my current view, it should be filed at the time that you've already been given the extension to and that matters relating to the new evidence can be added later. And I understand your arguments and that you would like to participate greatly in that brief, but nevertheless, we have already considered an extension. You've got the extension of 50-something days, as I recall, which is quite a substantial one. So you are in a situation really where we've got to get on with it. And your respondent's brief to the Prosecution's appellant's brief has to do with the facts as they were found by the Trial Chamber. So that doesn't involve what you were suggesting, that you would have to look at the whole question of genocide. You accept the findings but say the sentence imposed was not too low, in fact, it was too high, which you will be arguing in your appellant's brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a very simple --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, Your Honour, but the government's brief is an 80-page document, and to quote an American jurist, their argument on cumulative convictions, I think it was Judge Leonard Lernat Hand [phoen] who said, "Words are like pebbles in alien juxtaposition." That is an awfully high-flown way of saying that the government's brief on the cumulative conviction issue alone is very dense. And I don't mean this -- this is not a criticism. It's said with full recognition of the formidableness of the government's presentation. And I know that because my own personal schedule - and I apologise to Your Honour for invoking that. It's not my style. I don't like to do that, but I feel I have to now - I'm really not going to be able to take part in writing this brief if it's due December 21st. If Your Honour could see fit to grant us to at least January 10th and then, with as much conviction as I can muster, if you could give us some, certainly, reasonable period beyond that for our opening brief, I think we'll be able to submit an adequate brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cumulative convictions, of course, has been a matter which has been debated for a long time in this Tribunal. I was on the losing side in the decision which finally determined where the cumulative convictions should be imposed. So I have an interest in hearing what you might like to say. But the fact is that in the Celebici case, Delalic and others, the Appeals Chamber, by majority, gave a very detailed reasoning why in every case, notwithstanding the facts of the particular case, certain matters can be accumulated in convictions. Now, that is something which really we're all bound by. I wish somebody could upset it. I was rather proud of the judgement that I took part in, but nevertheless, it is not the law. The majority is the law, and it's a law which the Appeals Chamber will have to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If we have to submit the brief by December 21st, if that is Your Honour's final order, we will apologise in advance to Your Honour for submitting a work product that's going to be rather sketchy, and I say that with total respect for the Court. I think that the work product that will be submitted will not be something that we'll be particularly proud of, and I'm hoping that down the line -- I'm really sincerely requesting Your Honour on the January 10th deadline to consider that. Again, I don't think that we can get the quality of brief necessary in this case to Your Honours by January 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you accept the decision of the majority in the Celebici judgement and you simply deal with these particular crimes by applying the test which the majority judgement laid down, it is almost a mechanical process. That was one of the reasons why I thought it was wrong. But nevertheless, that's what's been laid down. Now, the Trial Chamber may have got that wrong, and we'd be very interested to hear whether they got it wrong in the application of that mechanical test. But that doesn't really require a great deal of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And believe me, Your Honour, you know much, much, much more about this than I do, and that's part of my problem. I've been in this case since October 19th. I still have cases that I'm trying to clear up in Portland. I can tell this to Your Honour: I have refused any other cases. I am not taking any new cases. This is absolutely my top priority. But Your Honour has reeled off a list of cases, and at least to this point, despite the fact that I have been working very, very diligently, I am not yet any kind of an expert in this area, nor am I in the genocide area, and the government has submitted some 50 pages or so, I believe it is, on the genocide issue which requires very serious reflection and analysis if we're to give the Court the aid that it suggests -- that it needs, rather. The case is not only important to General Krstic -- and by the way, in terms of his being in prison, I think it's fair to say that I believe that General Krstic has no problem with the request of his lawyers to obtain additional time. But this case is going to have very serious precendential value. I don't want to talk about anybody other than General Krstic. He is indeed our client. But I think it's obvious, particularly in terms of what went on today, Your Honour, this case is going to have very important precendential value in future cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that's why we will be looking forward to some very good advocacy when you come to argue the case before the Appeals Chamber. The briefs are the basic materials, but the case has to be litigated orally before the Appeals Chamber. And the difficulties that you say you are having in relation to the preparation of your written brief are matters that will obviously be taken into account, and I would think that if there is some reasonable explanation given, that if you need to add to it later, as a result of further studies, that you will be allowed to do so. But it's nevertheless, I'm afraid, a matter where we have to say this matter must proceed, and it may be that it will not be the perfect written document. But by the time we get on to the hearing of the appeal, one would expect you to be able to put it in the most perfectly clear set of propositions for us to deal with, and I should imagine that at that stage your understanding of the case will be a lot better. And you're not going to be punished if there is something that you want to change in your appellant's brief, but we must move on. So I don't propose to change the 21st for the response to the Prosecution's appellant's brief, the 24th for the more detailed reply to the Prosecution's response to your motion. But at the moment, we've got to get on with the appellant's briefs and the respondent's briefs in the two appeals. I will give you a decision on the issue of the extension of time for your own brief as soon as possible, hopefully by the end of this week. If not, it will be by, hopefully, somewhere between Christmas and New Year. But you will get -- I think you had better proceed upon the basis that your chances of getting a further extension are a little remote, but that's something I have to discuss with the other Judges. Yes, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just one matter. There were two things that you raised with respect to their reply. I just wanted to raise them. One, there was no argument made in their motion for the production of evidence as to why an oral hearing was necessary, so our response was simply that there's no argument put forward. You've asked now that that be placed in their reply, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. I've asked them to reply in more detail to your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies. My mistake, then. The other issue was that, unless I'm incorrect, you were referring to the legitimate forensic purpose test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The basis of the application is the failure under Rule 68 and the legal application of Rule 66 to appeals. If they do make reference to that, then, of course, if it's necessary, I just wanted to indicate that we didn't address those issues. That's my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you have any problem with that, if they raise it in their reply, we'll give you a chance to respond. I was rather surprised that in your response you don't appear to have referred them to the decision in Kordic, which said that Rule 66 does not apply after judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I apologise. I noticed that. I also noticed the other decision with respect to the extension of time, both in Kordic and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you were in it, as I recall. All right, then. We'll adjourn now.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
